status.en: 20 armed incidents reported in the past seven days, 100% more than the week before, most of them in La Espriella, Espriella and Catatumbo.
status.nb: 20 væpnede hendelser meldt de siste sju dagene, 100 prosent flere enn uken før, flest i La Espriella, Espriella og Catatumbo.

summary.en: Colombia opened an embassy in Jerusalem while UN independent experts urged Ecopetrol to provide reparations to armed-conflict victims, and the UN Security Council heard calls for the peace deal to endure as insecurity grows. Opposition groups launched protests against de la Espriella’s budget cuts, and the peace tribunal charged former FARC members with anti-Indigenous crimes. Budget cuts threaten the peace court and searches for the disappeared, officials say. Rebels detonated a car bomb outside a toll booth in Cauca, and FARC dissidents were killed in a Catatumbo operation and an army airstrike that also hit a teenager. 225 battle-related deaths were recorded in 2024, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Colombia åpnet en ambassade i Jerusalem mens FN-uavhengige eksperter oppfordret Ecopetrol til å yte erstatning til ofre for væpnet konflikt, og FNs sikkerhetsråd hørte oppfordringer om at fredsavtalen skal holde i møte med økende usikkerhet. Opposisjonsgrupper startet protester mot de la Espriellas budsjettkutt, og fredsdomstolen anklaget tidligere FARC-medlemmer for anti-urfolksforbrytelser. Budsjettkutt truer fredsretten og søk etter de savnede, sier myndighetene. Rebeller detonerte en bilbombe utenfor en bomstasjon i Cauca, og FARC-dissidenter ble drept i en operasjon i Catatumbo og i et luftangrep fra hæren som også traff en tenåring. 225 dødsfall knyttet til kamper ble registrert i 2024, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Colombian conflict
background.extract: The Colombian conflict began on May 27, 1964, and is a low-intensity asymmetric war between the government of Colombia, paramilitary groups, crime syndicates, and far-left guerrilla groups engaged in armed factional hostilities to increase their influence in Colombian territory. Some of the most important international contributors to the Colombian conflict include multinational corporations, the United States, Cuba, and the drug trafficking industry.
